title: Judgments like deep or powerful reflect the structure of the theorem network

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Judgments like deep or powerful reflect the structure of the theorem network

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Mathematicians' intuitive descriptions of theorems (difficult, powerful, surprising, deep) reflect features of the network of statements connected by theorems, and fields regarded as more successful should have more compact networks while fields full of isolated facts, such as elementary number theory, should have sparser networks.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And my suspicion is that our intuitive characterizations of theorems are in effect just reflections of our perception of various features of the structure of this network.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 820. Scope: networks of theorems and proofs in fields of mathematics

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-45: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.45

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing proof libraries allow network construction and proxy analyses, but direct intuitive labels and field-success measures are not contained in them. The hypothesis is testable only in restricted libraries or with new human-rating data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Build proof graphs from formal libraries, collect blinded ratings of theorem depth, power, surprise, and field success, then test preregistered associations with centrality, compression, and component density. Out-of-sample failure would refute specific network hypotheses.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many network metrics can be chosen post hoc.

Formal libraries are highly selected and uneven across fields.

Human judgments require new survey data for direct testing.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.35
analysis feasibility: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.48
data existence: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.4

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Proof libraries are public graphs of statements and dependencies, so network compactness can be measured for mathematics that has been formalized. They do not contain a controlled set of intuitive labels, and they are a biased sample of fields that formalize well. The comparison with elementary number theory is a partial proxy for the suspicion about sparser networks.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Build the dependence graph of a formal library, measure reuse and path-shortening, and compare those measures with independent ratings of depth or power and with a contrast between a compact algebraic field and elementary number theory. Agreement would support the suspicion; a reversed pattern would challenge it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Formal libraries over-represent fields chosen for formalization, which favors compact networks.

A successful area is partly identified by the same judgments the network is asked to explain.

There is no public dataset of mathematicians' ratings for difficult, powerful, surprising, or deep.
